sections.h2: Who qualifies for the Property Tax/Rent Rebate
sections.html:
Pennsylvania homeowners and renters qualify when they fit one of three age or disability groups and keep household income at or under $48,110 a year. The Department of Revenue runs the program, and gaming revenue pays for it.

  • Adults 65 and older.
  • Widows and widowers 50 and older.
  • People with disabilities 18 and older.

The income cap rose under Act 7 of 2023, which brought nearly 175,000 more people into eligibility. The program began in 1971, and older and disabled adults have received over $9.2 billion in property tax and rent relief since then.

sections.h2: How much the rebate pays at each income level
sections.html:
A standard rebate runs from $380 to $1,000, and the amount falls as household income rises. Four income bands set the payment.

Standard rebate by household income
Household incomeMaximum standard rebate
$0 to $8,550$1,000
$8,551 to $16,040$770
$16,041 to $19,240$460
$19,241 to $48,110$380

Most claimants land in the widest band, which spans everything from $19,241 up to the $48,110 cap. A household at the top of that band still receives the $380 rebate.

The supplement adds $190 to $500 on top of the standard rebate for applicants with the greatest need, and the Department figures it automatically from the claim. Two groups can receive it.

  • Property owners with income of $32,070 or less whose property taxes are more than 15% of that income.
  • Applicants who live in Philadelphia, Scranton or Pittsburgh.

Added to the standard rebate, the supplement lifts the top payment to $1,500 in the lowest income band. The next bands reach $1,155 and $690, and the band from $19,241 to $32,070 reaches $570. Nobody files a separate form for the supplement.

sections.h2: Documents that prove age, income and taxes paid
sections.html:
The claim needs four kinds of proof: age, income, tax or rent paid, and the school district code for your county. Photocopies are accepted for age.

  • Age: a birth certificate, driver's license or PA identification card, passport, Medicare card, PACE or PACENET card, hospital birth record, church baptismal record, or military or naturalization papers that show age.
  • Homeowners: receipted tax bills for the year being claimed.
  • Renters: a rent certificate filled in by the landlord or the landlord's agent. If the landlord's signature cannot be obtained, a rent certificate with a notarized affidavit works.
  • Income records for the claim year.

When a lender pays your bill from escrow, ask your local tax collector's office for a receipted copy. Keep these records with the claim, since the same set is needed again each year.

sections.h2: Extra schedules that go with the PA-1000 claim
sections.html:
Most applicants file only the PA-1000, but several situations call for an added schedule.

  • PA-1000 RC: renters.
  • PA-1000 A: someone who owned more than one home during the year, or an applicant who has died.
  • PA-1000 B/D/E: a widow or widower aged 50 to 64 who remarried, a renter who receives cash public assistance, or an owner who ran a business or rented out part of the home.
  • PA-1000 F/G: more than one eligible person on the deed or lease, or a deceased applicant.
  • PA-1000 PS: a physician's confirmation of permanent and total disability.
  • DEX-41: a claim filed for someone who has died.

Estates getting a Pennsylvania house ready for sale often meet the last three items, because a parent or spouse may have died before the claim was filed.

Claims for the 2025 year are due December 31, 2026, and an application postmarked by that day is accepted. Later claim years carry their own deadline, posted on the Department's program page.

The calendar repeats each cycle. Automated calls confirming receipt begin in April, and calls confirming approval begin in June. Rebates start going out July 1 by direct deposit or mailed check, whichever you chose on the application.

File online through mypath.pa.gov, by mail, or in person. Hundreds of in-person help sites around the state assist with the form at no charge.

A filed claim passes three milestones: a receipt call in April, an approval call in June, and payment beginning July 1. The calls are automated and reach applicants by phone.

The Department compares your age or disability category, income and tax or rent figure against the documents you attach. A disability claim also needs the physician's PA-1000 PS confirmation that the condition is permanent and total, so ask your doctor for it early.

Payment goes out in the form you picked on the application, either direct deposit or a mailed check. If your address or bank details change between years, correct them on the next application.

If you are selling the home during the claim year, keep the receipted tax bills and your income records together. The claim covers the year you owned and paid, and the paperwork is easier to gather before you move.

A straightforward claim goes in this order. First, pick the group you belong to: age 65 or older, widowed at 50 or older, or disabled at 18 or older. Second, add up household income for the claim year and compare it with the $48,110 cap. Third, collect proof of age, receipted tax bills or a rent certificate, and income records. Fourth, check whether any extra schedule applies to your situation, such as one for a renter, a second home or a deceased applicant. Fifth, file online at mypath.pa.gov, by mail, or at an in-person help site, and choose direct deposit or a mailed check.

Then wait for the receipt call in April and the approval call in June. If you do not hear anything or the figures look wrong, call the Department of Revenue rather than refiling. Keep a copy of everything you mailed, since the same documents are needed again next year.

sections.h2: Checking status and avoiding scam calls
sections.html:
Call the Department of Revenue at 1-888-PATAXES (728-2937) to check a claim, or use the online status tool. Have the primary applicant's Social Security number, date of birth and claim year ready. General program questions go to 1-888-222-9190.

Past applicants have received calls from scammers. The Department will never ask for bank account information by phone. Report callers who do to the Office of Attorney General.

faqs.q: Do I have to reapply for the rebate every year?
faqs.a: Yes. If you still meet the rules, you file a new application each year, because the amount depends on that year's income and the tax or rent you paid. Past applicants usually receive a booklet or reminder letter in the mail.

faqs.q: What is the most a Pennsylvania resident can receive?
faqs.a: The standard rebate tops out at $1,000. With the supplement, the lowest income band can reach $1,500, for owners who meet the 15% tax-to-income test or people living in Philadelphia, Scranton or Pittsburgh.
Yes. Renters file the PA-1000 with Schedule RC, which carries a rent certificate from the landlord. A notarized affidavit replaces the landlord's signature when it cannot be obtained.

faqs.q: Can someone claim the rebate for a person who has died?
faqs.a: Yes. A claim for a deceased applicant uses form DEX-41 together with Schedule A or F/G, depending on the situation. An estate's representative should read the form instructions before filing.

faqs.q: How do I find free help with the application?
faqs.a: Call 1-888-222-9190 or look up an in-person help site through the Department of Revenue. Hundreds of locations across Pennsylvania help applicants fill out the claim.
